title: Start of a Redirect Loop
statement:
When a user clicks an ad, the click goes through a chain of tracking redirects: each URL sends the browser to the next one until it reaches the landing page. A misconfigured campaign can create a redirect loop, where the chain comes back to a URL it already visited and never ends. You must find the URL where the loop starts, so it can be fixed.

The chain is a linked list stored as nxt: URL i redirects to URL nxt[i], and nxt[i] == -1 means URL i is the landing page (the end). The click always starts at URL 0. An empty list [] means there is no chain. URLs that the walk from 0 never reaches are ignored.

Write def solution(nxt) that returns the index of the first URL on the walk from 0 that is part of the loop (the URL the loop jumps back to), or -1 if the walk reaches an end. Use O(1) extra memory: no set or dict of visited URLs.

examples.why: The LeetCode 142 example 1 (pos = 1): 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 1 → ... The loop is 1, 2, 3 and the walk enters it at 1.
The LeetCode 142 example 2 (pos = 0): 0 → 1 → 0. The whole chain is the loop.
The LeetCode 142 example 3: one URL that is the landing page. No loop.

think.q: What shapes can the walk from URL 0 take?
think.a: Each URL has exactly one next URL, so the walk is a straight line. Either it hits -1 (no loop), or it repeats a URL, and from then on it goes round the same loop forever. That makes a 'rho' shape: a tail of a URLs, then a loop of L URLs. You want the first URL of the loop.

think.q: Run two walkers on [1, 2, 3, 1]: slow moves 1 hop, fast moves 2. Where do they meet?
think.a: Start both at 0. Step 1: slow 1, fast 2. Step 2: slow 2, fast 1 (2 → 3 → 1). Step 3: slow 3, fast 3. They meet at 3, which is not the loop start (1). So meeting tells you a loop exists, but you need one more phase to find where it starts.

think.q: What is the first idea that works?
think.a: Walk from 0 and put every URL in a set. The first URL you see twice is the loop start. That is O(n) time but O(n) memory, and the task forbids it.

Two pointers at different speeds (Floyd's tortoise and hare). Phase 1: slow moves 1, fast moves 2; they meet inside the loop if there is one, and fast hits -1 if not. Phase 2: put slow back at 0, leave fast at the meeting point, move both 1 hop at a time. They meet exactly at the loop start.

1. If nxt is empty, return -1.
  2. slow = fast = 0. Loop: if nxt[fast] or nxt[nxt[fast]] is -1, return -1. Else move slow 1 and fast 2; stop when they are equal.
  3. Set slow = 0.
  4. While slow != fast: move each 1 hop.
  5. Return slow.

Empty list. One URL that points to itself ([0], answer 0). A chain with no loop, of odd and even length (fast must check both of its hops). A loop that is the whole list (answer 0). A self-loop at the very end. A long tail with a short loop, and a short tail with a long loop. URLs in a shuffled order. A loop among URLs that 0 never reaches (answer -1).

hints: With a set it is easy. To use O(1) memory, think of two walkers at different speeds: if there is a loop, the fast one must eventually lap the slow one.
Before moving fast, check nxt[fast] != -1 and nxt[nxt[fast]] != -1. If either fails there is no loop. Otherwise move slow 1 hop, fast 2 hops, until they are equal.
After they meet, move slow back to URL 0 and step both one hop at a time. Write the distances: the tail length a equals a whole number of loops minus the meeting point's offset. Where do they meet?
brute:
def solution(nxt):
    # Walk from node 0 and remember every node. The first repeat is the loop start.
    # O(n) time but O(n) extra memory, which is what Floyd avoids.
    seen = set()
    node = 0 if nxt else -1
    while node != -1:
        if node in seen:
            return node
        seen.add(node)
        node = nxt[node]
    return -1
explain:
Example 1, [1, 2, 3, 1]: tail a = 1 (URL 0), loop L = 3 (URLs 1, 2, 3).

  • Phase 1: (slow, fast) goes (0, 0) → (1, 2) → (2, 1) → (3, 3). They meet at 3, which is b = 2 hops into the loop.
  • Phase 2: slow = 0, fast = 3. One hop each: slow 1, fast 1. Equal: return 1.

Why it works: when they meet, slow has walked a + b hops and fast has walked twice that, 2(a + b). Fast's extra a + b hops were whole laps of the loop, so a + b = kL for some whole number k. That means a = kL - b. Walking a hops from the meeting point (which is b into the loop) lands at b + kL - b = kL hops into the loop, which is the loop start. Walking a hops from URL 0 also lands at the loop start. So two walkers at the same speed, one from 0 and one from the meeting point, meet exactly there. Here a = 1, b = 2, L = 3, k = 1.

Phase 1 ends within about a + L steps, because once slow is in the loop, fast closes the gap by 1 each step. Total O(n) time and only two integers of memory.

perf.label: performance: 100,000 URLs, a tail of 60,000 then a loop of 40,000

talk: Phase 1 detects the loop: slow moves 1, fast moves 2. With a loop, fast gains 1 hop per step inside it, so it catches slow within one lap. Without one, fast hits -1, so I check nxt[fast] and nxt[nxt[fast]] before every move.

Why resetting one pointer to the head finds the start: at the meeting, slow walked a + b and fast 2(a + b), and the difference is whole laps, so a + b = kL, i.e. a = kL - b. Walking a more hops from the meeting point completes the lap to the loop start, and walking a hops from the head reaches the loop start too. So they meet there.
The set version is three lines and O(n) memory; Floyd keeps two ints. On a real linked list I would compare nodes with is; here nodes are indices, so == on ints is the same thing.
Edge cases I test: empty list, a self-loop [0], the whole list as a loop (answer 0 after phase 2 with zero steps), and odd and even lengths without a loop.
extensions: Also return the loop length: keep fast at the meeting point and count hops until slow comes back to it.
Just say whether a loop exists (LC 141): stop after phase 1.
Break the loop so the chain ends: walk from the loop start to the URL whose nxt is the loop start and set it to -1.

Real redirects are URLs, not indices: next_url is a dict from string to string, with None at the end. What changes, and does Floyd still need O(1) memory if you have to call an HTTP endpoint for each hop?
Find the Duplicate Number (LC 287): an array of n + 1 values in 1..n is a nxt list in disguise. Why is the duplicate the loop start?
